results.answer: A binary indexed tree stores at each index k the sum of a range of length p(k)=k&‑k that ends at k, so a prefix sum (1,k) can be obtained by adding together the O(log n) stored ranges that partition [1,k]. The algorithm repeatedly adds tree[k] to an accumulator and moves to the next relevant index with k ← k − (k&‑k) until k = 0, yielding the prefix sum in O(log n) time【3】【4】.

A segment tree has only O(log n) levels, so a range query climbs at most one level per step and visits only a logarithmic number of nodes. Consequently the total work is proportional to the height of the tree, giving O(log n) time for a query【4】【5】.

The union‑find structure determines that two elements are in the same set by finding each element’s representative and checking whether the representatives are identical (e.g., `same(a,b)` returns `find(a)==find(b)`)【4】【5】

The Z‑algorithm processes the string from left to right while maintaining the rightmost interval [x, y] such that s[x…y] is a prefix of s. For each position k it first checks the previously stored value z[k‑x]; if k + z[k‑x] < y the Z‑value can be copied (z[k] = z[k‑x]), otherwise the algorithm compares characters beyond y to extend the match and updates the interval [x, y] accordingly, guaranteeing O(n) time. [1][3]

Topological sorting yields an ordering of the graph’s nodes such that whenever there is a path from node a to node b, node a precedes node b in the list. Every directed acyclic graph (DAG) therefore has at least one such topological order. [1][2]

Jumping to the middle repeatedly halves the remaining region to search, so each step eliminates half of the possible positions and the algorithm finishes in O(log n) time. In contrast, walking through the list one element at a time examines each element sequentially, requiring O(n) steps in the worst case. [2]

You can compute a hash value for each piece of text (e.g., using polynomial hashing that combines character codes with chosen constants) and then compare the two hash values instead of the characters themselves【2】. After an O(n) preprocessing step you can obtain any substring’s hash in O(1) time, allowing fast equality checks, though a collision—different texts with the same hash—is possible but unlikely with carefully chosen parameters【1】【3】.

Yes. An Eulerian path is a walk that traverses each edge of a graph exactly once, and it exists when all edges lie in a single connected component and either every node has even degree or exactly two nodes have odd degree (the odd‑degree nodes become the start and end of the path)【1】【2】.

Pick any node a in the tree, run a depth‑first (or breadth‑first) search to find the node b that is farthest from a. Then start a second search from b and find the node c that is farthest from b; the pair (b, c) are the two points whose distance is the tree’s diameter, i.e., the farthest apart points in the branching structure【2】. This two‑search method works because the longest path in a tree always has its endpoints at the farthest nodes discovered in this way【2】.

Keep a monotonic queue (deque) of the window’s elements. When the window moves, discard from the back any elements larger than the new entry, push the new entry onto the back, and pop the front if its element has slid out of the window; the element at the front is then the current minimum. This lets you update the minimum in O(1) per step, giving an overall O(n) algorithm [1][3][4].

Amortized analysis looks at the total time spent by all operations in a sequence and spreads the cost of any occasional expensive operation over the many cheap ones, so the average (amortized) cost per operation remains low【1】【3】.

Picking the largest‑value coin first can be wrong for non‑canonical coin systems; for example, with coins {1, 3, 4} and target 6 the greedy choice gives 4 + 1 + 1, while the optimal solution is 3 + 3 [1].  The failure is avoided by solving the problem with dynamic programming, which computes the minimum‑coin solution for any coin set [2].

Beyond simple range‑sum queries, a segment tree can be constructed to answer many other operations, such as minimum and maximum queries, greatest‑common‑divisor queries, and bit‑wise operations (AND, OR, XOR) on a range【2】【1】.

Both structures answer range‑query and point‑update operations in O(log n) time, but a binary indexed tree is limited to sum queries while a segment tree can handle many other associative queries (e.g., min, max) and even range updates via lazy propagation【1†L1-L4】【2†L1-L4】. Because a BIT is simpler to implement and uses less memory, it is preferred when only prefix‑sum or range‑sum queries are needed; a segment tree is chosen when the problem requires more general queries or range‑update capabilities despite its higher memory cost and implementation complexity【2†L4-L6】.
